Choosing the Number of Classes

Source: vignettes/class_enumeration.Rmd
class_enumeration.Rmd
library(mixtureEM)

Every latent class analysis starts with the same question: how many classes? There is no single decisive statistic, so the standard practice is to fit a range of solutions and weigh several kinds of evidence together (Nylund et al., 2007):

  1. Information criteria (BIC, SABIC, AIC) — lower is better.
  2. The bootstrap likelihood ratio test (BLRT) — a formal test of k classes against k − 1.
  3. Classification quality (entropy, average posterior probabilities).
  4. Absolute and local fit — does the chosen model actually reproduce the data?
  5. Interpretability and class sizes — a smallest class under 5% of the sample, or with fewer than about 25 cases, is one you have to be able to defend on substantive grounds, however much it improves the BIC (Lee et al., 2023). That is a reporting convention, not a rule; mixtureEM applies no minimum and will happily estimate a class of three people.

This vignette walks through all five on a classic dataset: poLCA::carcinoma, in which seven pathologists each rated the same 118 biopsy slides for the presence of carcinoma (Agresti, 2002). The question a latent class model asks here is: how many types of slide are there, given how the raters agree and disagree?

The chunks below run only if the poLCA package is installed (install.packages("poLCA")).

The data 

data(carcinoma, package = "poLCA")
# poLCA codes ratings 1/2; recode to 0/1 for measurement = "binary".
ratings <- as.matrix(carcinoma) - 1
head(ratings)
#>      A B C D E F G
#> [1,] 0 0 0 0 0 0 0
#> [2,] 0 0 0 0 0 0 0
#> [3,] 0 0 0 0 0 0 0
#> [4,] 0 0 0 0 0 0 0
#> [5,] 0 0 0 0 0 0 0
#> [6,] 0 0 0 0 0 0 0

Information criteria

compare_mixtures() fits each candidate number of classes and prints the information criteria side by side:

set.seed(1)
selection <- compare_mixtures(ratings, k_range = 1:5,
                              measurement = "binary", n_init = 20)
#> Running Model Selection across K = 1 to 5...
#> 
#> Fitting 1-class model...
#> Fitting 2-class model...
#> Fitting 3-class model...
#> Fitting 4-class model...
#> Fitting 5-class model...
#> 
#> === Model Selection Summary ===
#>   Classes       LL Params      AIC      BIC    SABIC Entropy Unreplicated
#> 1       1 -524.465      7 1062.930 1082.324 1060.196   1.000        FALSE
#> 2       2 -318.159     15  666.318  707.878  660.459   0.963        FALSE
#> 3       3 -294.935     23  635.869  699.595  626.886   0.915        FALSE
#> 4       4 -290.739     31  643.478  729.369  631.370   0.852        FALSE
#> 5       5 -288.512     39  655.025  763.082  639.793   0.862        FALSE
#> 
#> -> Best model according to BIC: 3 classes

BIC prefers three classes here — the solution the methodological literature has repeatedly recovered for these data: clearly negative slides, clearly positive slides, and an ambiguous group the raters split on.

The bootstrap likelihood ratio test

The BLRT asks the sharper question “does adding one more class fit significantly better?”, with the null distribution generated by parametric bootstrap (McLachlan & Peel, 2000). It is slow, because each replication refits both models; keep n_reps modest while exploring. A test you intend to report is a different matter: refit it at n_reps = 999. A bootstrap p-value can only take the values 1/(B + 1), 2/(B + 1), …, so at 50 or 100 draws it cannot separate .04 from .06, and blrt() warns when the result lands that close to the line. See vignette("estimation") for the power figures behind those numbers.

set.seed(2)
blrt_23 <- blrt(ratings, k_small = 2, k_large = 3,
                measurement = "binary", n_reps = 50, verbose = FALSE)
blrt_23
#> =========================================================
#>        BOOTSTRAP LIKELIHOOD RATIO TEST (BLRT)            
#> =========================================================
#>   Comparison       : 2 vs 3 classes
#>   Log-Likelihoods  : -318.16 (2-class) -> -294.93 (3-class)
#>   LR statistic     : 46.45
#>   Bootstrap draws  : 50
#> ---------------------------------------------------------
#>   Bootstrap p      : p = 0.020
#>   Conclusion       : the 3-class model fits significantly better.
#> =========================================================

set.seed(3)
blrt_34 <- blrt(ratings, k_small = 3, k_large = 4,
                measurement = "binary", n_reps = 50, verbose = FALSE)
blrt_34
#> =========================================================
#>        BOOTSTRAP LIKELIHOOD RATIO TEST (BLRT)            
#> =========================================================
#>   Comparison       : 3 vs 4 classes
#>   Log-Likelihoods  : -294.93 (3-class) -> -290.74 (4-class)
#>   LR statistic     : 8.39
#>   Bootstrap draws  : 50
#> ---------------------------------------------------------
#>   Bootstrap p      : p = 0.137
#>   Conclusion       : no significant improvement over the 3-class model.
#> =========================================================

The 2-vs-3 test rejects (a third class is needed); the 3-vs-4 test does not, agreeing with BIC.

Classification quality and fit of the chosen model 

set.seed(4)
fit <- fit_mixture(ratings, n_classes = 3, measurement = "binary", n_init = 30)
fit

Which entropy is being reported

Relative entropy is an absolute entropy expressed on a 0-1 scale, and there is more than one convention for the denominator that puts it there. mixtureEM divides by nlog⁡Kn \log K, the entropy of a uniform distribution over the KK classes — the largest value the absolute entropy could take. Some other implementations divide instead by nH(π̂)n H(\hat\pi), the entropy of the estimated class sizes. Both appear in the literature and neither is wrong, but they do not give the same number, so an entropy quoted from elsewhere is not always comparable with the one printed here.

Because H(π̂)≤log⁡KH(\hat\pi) \le \log K always, with equality only when the classes come out exactly equal in size, the figure reported here is always the higher of the two. The gap is small for balanced solutions and grows as the class sizes become uneven. To convert:

Rother2=1−(1−Rhere2)log⁡KH(π̂),H(π)=−∑kπklog⁡πkR^2_{\text{other}} = 1 - (1 - R^2_{\text{here}}) \frac{\log K}{H(\hat\pi)}, \qquad H(\pi) = -\sum_k \pi_k \log \pi_k

Either way, entropy describes how cleanly a solution separates cases; it is not evidence for how many classes there are. A model can separate two classes beautifully and still be the wrong model.

Absolute fit compares the observed response-pattern frequencies with the model-implied ones, and the bivariate residuals localise any misfit to specific pairs of items:

absolute_fit(fit)
#> =========================================================
#>                   ABSOLUTE FIT                           
#> =========================================================
#> Table: 128 cells, 20 observed response patterns
#> Free parameters: 23   df: 104
#> 
#> Statistic               Value    p-value
#> ---------------------------------------- 
#> L-squared             17.7208     1.0000
#> X-squared             21.1127     1.0000
#> Cressie-Read          18.5874     1.0000
#> Dissimilarity          0.1170           
#> =========================================================
#> Note: the table is sparse, so the chi-square reference
#>  distribution is unreliable. Prefer these statistics for
#>  comparing models over testing one in isolation.
bivariate_residuals(fit)
#> =========================================================
#>                BIVARIATE RESIDUALS                       
#> =========================================================
#> Pearson chi-square per item pair, divided by its df.
#> Ranks which pairs strain the model. NOT a calibrated
#> test: referred to chi-square this statistic almost
#> never rejects, so a low value is not evidence of fit.
#> Use n_reps for bootstrap p-values.
#> 
#>          A        B        C        D        E        F
#> B   0.1035
#> C   0.3456   0.0024
#> D   0.7983   0.7643   0.0062
#> E   0.0937   0.0890   0.3741   0.4804
#> F   0.1803   0.6055   0.0076   4.6889   0.2012
#> G   0.2487   0.1070   0.3273   0.6427   0.1952   0.1729
#> 
#> Largest: F x D = 4.6889
#> Total BVR: 10.4345
#> =========================================================

Finally, the profile plot is the interpretability check — three classes that are well separated and substantively meaningful:

plot(fit, class_labels = c("Negative", "Positive", "Ambiguous"),
     main = "Pathologist agreement (3-class LCA)")

References

Agresti, A. (2002). Categorical data analysis (2nd ed.). Wiley.

Lee, T. K., Wickrama, K. A. S., & O’Neal, C. W. (2023). An introduction to growth mixture models (GMM). In International Encyclopedia of Education (4th ed., Vol. 14, pp. 646–655). Elsevier. https://doi.org/10.1016/B978-0-12-818630-5.10076-4

McLachlan, G., & Peel, D. (2000). Finite mixture models. Wiley.

Sclove, S. L. (1987). Application of model-selection criteria to some problems in multivariate analysis. Psychometrika, 52(3), 333–343. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02294360

Nylund, K. L., Asparouhov, T., & Muthén, B. O. (2007). Deciding on the number of classes in latent class analysis and growth mixture modeling: A Monte Carlo simulation study. Structural Equation Modeling, 14(4), 535–569. https://doi.org/10.1080/10705510701575396
